reason: This was the one that nearly fell. The web evidence is split: Shmoop, Study.com and the general run of study sites print "It's when you know you're licked before you begin, but you begin anyway and see it through no matter what", with a comma before "but" and without the second "you". The verifier could not open a Lippincott copy and cited a single online full text, which put the line one witness deep against a popular contrary reading. So I went to scanned printed books. The americanliterature.com page is behind a Cloudflare challenge and cannot be read, so I found two independent Internet Archive scans of printed copies (items tkmfull-text and to-kill-a-mockingbird-harper-lee-book) and downloaded both OCR texts. They agree with each other and with the proposal, word for word and mark for mark: "I wanted you to see what real courage is, instead of getting the idea that courage is a man with a gun in his hand. It's when you know you're licked before you begin but you begin anyway and you see it through no matter what. You rarely win, but sometimes you do. Mrs. Dubose won, all ninety-eight pounds of her." No comma before "but", and "and you see it through". The study-site reading is the misquotation; the proposal has the book. The locator is right by count, not by trust: in the first scan the passage stands at line 6793, after the opening of chapter 11 ("When we were small, Jem and I confined our activities to the southern neighborhood", line 5993) and before the opening of chapter 12 ("Jem was twelve", line 6822), and the second scan brackets it the same way. The occasion is right: Atticus is explaining what the reading aloud was for, after Mrs Dubose's death. Speaker named, and it is his own line, not reported of another. Lee is not banned, not on the misattribution list, stands at one of three (month 2), and shipped.js returns no shipped or near match. In scope: a novel of 1960, publishable, no content warning needed. Tag Fiction is the form. Source line 89 characters, name first, no dash, curly apostrophes. The honest gap the verifier declares stands and is not a defect: no Lippincott 1960 copy was opened, which is why the source names the year and no publisher, and the two printings I read are later ones. The wording is now attested in print twice over rather than on one website.
